§1926.1400 Scope Coverage starts with power-operated equipment used in construction that can hoist, lower and horizontally move a suspended load. The list includes many crane types, derricks, dedicated pile drivers, service/mechanic trucks with a hoisting device, and variations, and it is not exhaustive [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Multi-purpose machines are listed when configured to do this with a winch or hook [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Attachments, whether crane-attached or suspended, don't remove covered equipment from scope [29cfr1926.1400(b)].

Check the exclusions. Machinery converted for non-hoisting use is excluded while so converted [29cfr1926.1400(c)(1)]. Excavators, backhoes, power shovels and listed loaders are excluded even when lifting with rigging [29cfr1926.1400(c)(2)]. Forklifts are excluded except when configured to hoist with a winch or hook and move a suspended load [29cfr1926.1400(c)(8)]. A mechanic's truck is excluded when used in equipment maintenance and repair activities [29cfr1926.1400(c)(9)]. Wreckers, digger derricks, aerial devices, tree work and other listed items also have exclusions, some conditional [29cfr1926.1400(c)]. Digger derrick work under subpart V or telecommunication construction must meet stated compliance conditions to qualify [29cfr1926.1400(c)(4)].

For articulating/knuckle-boom delivery cranes, ground transfer is excluded when materials aren't arranged in a particular sequence for hoisting [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(i)]. Placing building supply sheet goods or packaged materials onto a structure is excluded when using a boom-end fork/cradle, "but only when the truck crane is equipped with a properly functioning automatic overload prevention device" [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(ii)]. The exclusion doesn't apply when holding, supporting or stabilizing material to facilitate construction [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(A)], or when handling prefabricated components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(B)] or structural steel members or systems-engineered metal building components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(C)].

Employers must establish, effectively communicate and enforce work rules ensuring compliance with provisions directing employee actions [29cfr1926.1400(f)]. Controlling entity duties include those in the sections named in [29cfr1926.1400(e)]. “Such attachments, whether crane-attached or suspended include, but are not limited to: Hooks, magnets, grapples, clamshell buckets, orange peel buckets, concrete buckets, drag lines, personnel platforms, augers or drills and pile driving equipment. (c) Exclusions. This subpart does not cover: (1) Machinery included in paragraph (a) of this section while it has been converted or adapted for a non-hoisting/lifting use. Such conversions/adaptations include, but are not limited to, power shovels, excavators and concrete pumps.”

For articulating/knuckle-boom delivery cranes, ground transfer is excluded when materials aren't arranged in a particular sequence for hoisting [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(i)]. Placing building supply sheet goods or packaged materials onto a structure is excluded when using a boom-end fork/cradle, "but only when the truck crane is equipped with a properly functioning automatic overload prevention device" [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(ii)]. The exclusion doesn't apply when holding, supporting or stabilizing material to facilitate construction [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(A)], or when handling prefabricated components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(B)] or structural steel members or systems-engineered metal building components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(C)].

Employers must establish, effectively communicate and enforce work rules ensuring compliance with provisions directing employee actions [29cfr1926.1400(f)]. Controlling entity duties include those in the sections named in [29cfr1926.1400(e)]. “(5) Machinery originally designed as vehicle-mounted aerial devices (for lifting personnel) and self-propelled elevating work platforms. (6) Telescopic/hydraulic gantry systems. (7) Stacker cranes. (8) Powered industrial trucks (forklifts), except when configured to hoist and lower (by means of a winch or hook) and horizontally move a suspended load.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Moving point-to-point means the times during which an employee is in the process of going to or from a work station. Multi-purpose machine means a machine that is designed to be configured in various ways, at least one of which allows it to hoist (by means of a winch or hook) and horizontally move a suspended load. For example, a machine that can rotate and can be configured with removable forks/tongs (for use as a forklift) or with a winch pack, jib (with a hook at the end) or jib used in conjunction with a winch.”

Employers using equipment covered by this subpart that meets the definition of “roadway maintenance machine,” as defined in 49 CFR 214.7, must comply with the requirements in this subpart, except as provided in paragraphs (b)(1) through (7) of this section when subject to the authority of the Federal Railroad Administration.” §1926.1400 Scope Coverage starts with power-operated equipment used in construction that can hoist, lower and horizontally move a suspended load. The list includes many crane types, derricks, dedicated pile drivers, service/mechanic trucks with a hoisting device, and variations, and it is not exhaustive [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Multi-purpose machines are listed when configured to do this with a winch or hook [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Attachments, whether crane-attached or suspended, don't remove covered equipment from scope [29cfr1926.1400(b)].

Check the exclusions. Machinery converted for non-hoisting use is excluded while so converted [29cfr1926.1400(c)(1)]. Excavators, backhoes, power shovels and listed loaders are excluded even when lifting with rigging [29cfr1926.1400(c)(2)]. Forklifts are excluded except when configured to hoist with a winch or hook and move a suspended load [29cfr1926.1400(c)(8)]. A mechanic's truck is excluded when used in equipment maintenance and repair activities [29cfr1926.1400(c)(9)]. Wreckers, digger derricks, aerial devices, tree work and other listed items also have exclusions, some conditional [29cfr1926.1400(c)]. Digger derrick work under subpart V or telecommunication construction must meet stated compliance conditions to qualify [29cfr1926.1400(c)(4)].

For articulating/knuckle-boom delivery cranes, ground transfer is excluded when materials aren't arranged in a particular sequence for hoisting [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(i)]. Placing building supply sheet goods or packaged materials onto a structure is excluded when using a boom-end fork/cradle, "but only when the truck crane is equipped with a properly functioning automatic overload prevention device" [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(ii)]. The exclusion doesn't apply when holding, supporting or stabilizing material to facilitate construction [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(A)], or when handling prefabricated components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(B)] or structural steel members or systems-engineered metal building components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(C)].

Employers must establish, effectively communicate and enforce work rules ensuring compliance with provisions directing employee actions [29cfr1926.1400(f)]. Controlling entity duties include those in the sections named in [29cfr1926.1400(e)]. “(b) Attachments. This standard applies to equipment included in paragraph (a) of this section when used with attachments. Such attachments, whether crane-attached or suspended include, but are not limited to: Hooks, magnets, grapples, clamshell buckets, orange peel buckets, concrete buckets, drag lines, personnel platforms, augers or drills and pile driving equipment. (c) Exclusions. This subpart does not cover: (1) Machinery included in paragraph (a) of this section while it has been converted or adapted for a non-hoisting/lifting use.” §1926.1400(f) “(f) Where provisions of this standard direct an operator, crewmember, or other employee to take certain actions, the employer must establish, effectively communicate to the relevant persons, and enforce, work rules to ensure compliance with such provisions.”

(a) General rule. Employers using equipment covered by this subpart that meets the definition of “roadway maintenance machine,” as defined in 49 CFR 214.7, must comply with the requirements in this subpart, except as provided in paragraphs (b)(1) through (7) of this section when subject to the authority of the Federal Railroad Administration.

The list includes many crane types, derricks, dedicated pile drivers, service/mechanic trucks with a hoisting device, and variations, and it is not exhaustive [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Multi-purpose machines are listed when configured to do this with a winch or hook [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Attachments, whether crane-attached or suspended, don't remove covered equipment from scope [29cfr1926.1400(b)].

Check the exclusions. Machinery converted for non-hoisting use is excluded while so converted [29cfr1926.1400(c)(1)]. Excavators, backhoes, power shovels and listed loaders are excluded even when lifting with rigging [29cfr1926.1400(c)(2)]. Forklifts are excluded except when configured to hoist with a winch or hook and move a suspended load [29cfr1926.1400(c)(8)]. A mechanic's truck is excluded when used in equipment maintenance and repair activities [29cfr1926.1400(c)(9)]. Wreckers, digger derricks, aerial devices, tree work and other listed items also have exclusions, some conditional [29cfr1926.1400(c)]. Digger derrick work under subpart V or telecommunication construction must meet stated compliance conditions to qualify [29cfr1926.1400(c)(4)].

For articulating/knuckle-boom delivery cranes, ground transfer is excluded when materials aren't arranged in a particular sequence for hoisting [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(i)]. Placing building supply sheet goods or packaged materials onto a structure is excluded when using a boom-end fork/cradle, "but only when the truck crane is equipped with a properly functioning automatic overload prevention device" [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(ii)]. The exclusion doesn't apply when holding, supporting or stabilizing material to facilitate construction [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(A)], or when handling prefabricated components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(B)] or structural steel members or systems-engineered metal building components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(C)].

(b) Attachments. This standard applies to equipment included in paragraph (a) of this section when used with attachments. Such attachments, whether crane-attached or suspended include, but are not limited to: Hooks, magnets, grapples, clamshell buckets, orange peel buckets, concrete buckets, drag lines, personnel platforms, augers or drills and pile driving equipment. response.text:
§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Dismantling includes partial dismantling (such as dismantling to shorten a boom or substitute a different component). Drum rotation indicator means a device on a crane or hoist which indicates in which direction and at what relative speed a particular hoist drum is turning. Electrical contact occurs when a person, object, or equipment makes contact or comes in close proximity with an energized conductor or equipment that allows the passage of current. Employer-made equipment means floating cranes/derricks designed and built by an employer for the employer's own use.” §1926.1437 Floating cranes/derricks and land cranes/derricks on barges This supplements the subpart for floating and barge-mounted cranes and derricks, excluding jacked barges fully supported by deployed jacks [29cfr1926.1437(a)]. Work area control applies except § 1926.1424(a)(2)(ii); use barriers, or signs plus equipment markings and employee training [29cfr1926.1437(c)]. § 1926.1425 doesn't apply [29cfr1926.1437(d)]. Add list/trim and house-lock devices, plus a wind indicator when a competent person finds wind relevant [29cfr1926.1437(e)]. Anti two-block applies only to personnel hoisting or hoisting over occupied cofferdams or shafts; listed work has load-weighing relief [29cfr1926.1437(f)]. Cab or no-cab information-access rules apply [29cfr1926.1437(g)].

Competent persons inspect the flotation each shift and monthly [29cfr1926.1437(h)(3)]. Annual external and four-year internal inspections require specified expertise; hazards remove the vessel from service, and flagged nonhazards are monitored [29cfr1926.1437(h)(4)] [29cfr1926.1437(h)(5)]. Document monthly, annual and four-year inspections; keep four-year records at least 4 years [29cfr1926.1437(h)(6)].

Diver work requires dedicated crane use until all divers return, continuous control attendance, tender sightline or electronic signals, and no-shift securing [29cfr1926.1437(j)]. Don't exceed vessel environmental, operating or transit limits [29cfr1926.1437(k)].

For permanent marine equipment, follow water charts and their parameters; charts consider minimum 40 mph wind [29cfr1926.1437(m)(1)]. List/trim maximums, in degrees, are 5 each at 25 tons or less, 7 over 25, and 10 for derricks [29cfr1926.1437-table-M1]. Stability: 60 mph with 2 ft freeboard at rated capacity or high boom/no load; 1 ft at capacity plus 25% [29cfr1926.1437-table-M2]; backward stability, high boom/no load/full back list, 90 mph [29cfr1926.1437-table-M3]. Employer-made equipment needs engineer-signed proof [29cfr1926.1437(m)(4)].

Land equipment needs expert derating [29cfr1926.1437(n)(2)]. Vessel list/trim cannot exceed the least of 5 degrees or the manufacturer's limit (qualified person's if unspecified), and must preserve above-water decks and a fully submerged bottom [29cfr1926.1437(n)(3)(i)] [29cfr1926.1437(n)(4)]. Crane list/trim limits also apply [29cfr1926.1437(n)(3)(ii)]. Secure by attachment, corral, rails or centerline cable, except qualifying mobile auxiliaries under a plan [29cfr1926.1437(n)]. Both equipment categories have hull requirements [29cfr1926.1437(m)(5)] [29cfr1926.1437(n)(7)]. “The requirements of this section do not apply when using jacked barges when the jacks are deployed to the river, lake, or sea bed and the barge is fully supported by the jacks. (b) General requirements. The requirements in paragraphs (c) through (k) of this section apply to both floating cranes/derricks and land cranes/derricks on barges, pontoons, vessels or other means of flotation. (c) Work area control. (1) The requirements of § 1926.1424 (Work area control) apply, except for § 1926.1424(a)(2)(ii).”

response.text:
§1926.1402(f) “(f) This section does not apply to cranes designed for use on railroad tracks when used on railroad tracks that are part of the general railroad system of transportation that is regulated pursuant to the Federal Railroad Administration under 49 CFR part 213 and that comply with applicable Federal Railroad Administration requirements.” §1926.1400(h) “(h) Section 1926.1402 does not apply to cranes designed for use on railroad tracks, when used on railroad tracks that are part of the general railroad system of transportation that is regulated pursuant to the Federal Railroad Administration under 49 CFR part 213, and that comply with applicable Federal Railroad Administration requirements. See § 1926.1402(f).” §1926.1402 Ground conditions Do not assemble or use the equipment unless the ground is firm, drained and graded enough to meet the manufacturer's specifications for adequate support and degree of level. You may count supporting materials, if necessary, toward meeting them. Drainage is not required in marshes or wetlands [29cfr1926.1402(b)]. Ground conditions include slope, compaction and firmness [29cfr1926.1402(a)(1)]. Supporting materials include blocking, mats, cribbing, marsh buggies in marshes or wetlands, and similar materials or devices [29cfr1926.1402(a)(2)].

The controlling entity must ensure the necessary ground preparations are provided [29cfr1926.1402(c)(1)]. It must also inform the equipment user and operator of the location of hazards beneath the set-up area, such as voids, tanks and utilities. The duty covers hazards identified in documents in its possession, on or off site, or hazards it otherwise knows about [29cfr1926.1402(c)(2)].

Without a controlling entity, the preparation duty in (c)(1) falls on the employer with authority at the site to make or arrange the preparations [29cfr1926.1402(d)].

If you, as operator, or the A/D director determine that conditions fall short, that person's employer must discuss the needed preparations with the controlling entity. The aim is to meet paragraph (b), using suitable supporting materials or devices if necessary [29cfr1926.1402(e)]. A limited exclusion applies to certain cranes on railroad tracks [29cfr1926.1402(f)]. “(f) This section does not apply to cranes designed for use on railroad tracks when used on railroad tracks that are part of the general railroad system of transportation that is regulated pursuant to the Federal Railroad Administration under 49 CFR part 213 and that comply with applicable Federal Railroad Administration requirements.”

§1926.1428 Signal person qualifications The signal person's employer must ensure each signal person meets the Qualification Requirements before giving any signals, using Option (1) or Option (2) [29cfr1926.1428(a)]. Option (1) relies on documentation from a third party qualified evaluator showing the person meets them [29cfr1926.1428(a)(1)]. Under Option (2), the employer's qualified evaluator assesses the person, determines that the requirements are met and documents that determination. This assessment "is not portable": other employers may not use it to meet this section [29cfr1926.1428(a)(2)].

Under either option, the documentation must be available at the site while the employer employs the signal person. It must specify each type of signaling, such as hand or radio signals, for which the person qualifies [29cfr1926.1428(a)(3)].

Qualification covers knowing the signals used, including the Standard Method if hand signals are used [29cfr1926.1428(c)(1)]; competence in applying them [29cfr1926.1428(c)(2)]; a basic understanding of equipment operation and limitations, including swing and stopping dynamics and boom deflection [29cfr1926.1428(c)(3)]; and the relevant requirements of §§ 1926.1419 through 1926.1422 and 1926.1428 [29cfr1926.1428(c)(4)]. These are demonstrated through an oral or written test and a practical test [29cfr1926.1428(c)(5)].

If later actions indicate a signal person does not qualify, the employer must not allow continued signaling work until retraining and a confirming re-assessment under paragraph (a) [29cfr1926.1428(b)]. “This requirement must be met by using either Option (1) or Option (2) of this section. §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “§ 1926.1401 Definitions. A/D director (Assembly/Disassembly director) means an individual who meets this subpart's requirements for an A/D director, irrespective of the person's formal job title or whether the person is non-management or management personnel. Articulating crane means a crane whose boom consists of a series of folding, pin connected structural members, typically manipulated to extend or retract by power from hydraulic cylinders.” §1926.1404 Assembly/Disassembly—general requirements (applies to all assembly and disassembly operations) Assembly/disassembly is directed by the A/D director: a competent and qualified person, or a competent person assisted by qualified persons. A lone worker must be both [29cfr1926.1404(a)]. Each time reliance is to be placed on the boom hoist brake to prevent boom movement during assembly/disassembly, the brake must be tested prior to such reliance to determine if it is sufficient to prevent boom movement. If it is not sufficient, a boom hoist pawl, other locking device/back-up braking device, or another method of preventing dangerous movement of the boom (such as blocking or using an assist crane) from a boom hoist brake failure must be used.” §1926.1430(c)(3)(i) “(i) On friction equipment, whenever moving a boom off a support, first raise the boom a short distance (sufficient to take the load of the boom) to determine if the boom hoist brake needs to be adjusted. See § 1926.1417(f) and (j) for additional requirements.” §1926.1426(b)(2) “(2) Hydraulic drums must have an integrally mounted holding device or internal static brake to prevent boom hoist movement in the event of hydraulic failure.”

body.text: §1926.1404(h)(10) Boom hoist brake failure

(10) Boom hoist brake failure. Each time reliance is to be placed on the boom hoist brake to prevent boom movement during assembly/disassembly, the brake must be tested prior to such reliance to determine if it is sufficient to prevent boom movement. If it is not sufficient, a boom hoist pawl, other locking device/back-up braking device, or another method of preventing dangerous movement of the boom (such as blocking or using an assist crane) from a boom hoist brake failure must be used.

(i) On friction equipment, whenever moving a boom off a support, first raise the boom a short distance (sufficient to take the load of the boom) to determine if the boom hoist brake needs to be adjusted. On other types of equipment with a boom, the same practice is applicable, except that typically there is no means of adjusting the brake; if the brake does not hold, a repair is necessary. See § 1926.1417(f) and (j) for additional requirements.
(2) Hydraulic drums must have an integrally mounted holding device or internal static brake to prevent boom hoist movement in the event of hydraulic failure.

§1926.1401 Definitions

These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Operator means a person who is operating the equipment. Overhead and gantry cranes includes overhead/bridge cranes, semigantry, cantilever gantry, wall cranes, storage bridge cranes, launching gantry cranes, and similar equipment, irrespective of whether it travels on tracks, wheels, or other means. Paragraph refers to a paragraph in the same section of this subpart that the word “paragraph” is used, unless otherwise specified. Pendants includes both wire and bar types. Wire type: A fixed length of wire rope with mechanical fittings at both ends for pinning segments of wire rope together.”

(B) Determine if any part of the equipment, load line or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), while operating up to the equipment's maximum working radius in the work zone, could get closer than the minimum approach distance of the power line permitted under Table A (see § 1926.1408).” §1926.1408(a)(2)(iii)(B) “(B) Determine if any part of the equipment, load line or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), while operating up to the equipment's maximum working radius in the work zone, could get closer than the minimum approach distance of the power line permitted under Table A (see § 1926.1408). If so, then the employer must follow the requirements in paragraph (b) of this section to ensure that no part of the equipment, load line, or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), gets closer to the line than the minimum approach distance.” §1926.1410 Power line safety (all voltages)—equipment operations closer than the Table A zone Operating inside the § 1926.1408 Table A distance is prohibited unless the employer demonstrates that all conditions are met [29cfr1926.1410]. The employer must determine that breaching it is unavoidable for feasibility reasons [29cfr1926.1410(a)] and, after consulting the utility, that deenergizing and grounding or relocating the line is infeasible [29cfr1926.1410(b)]. The line owner/operator or a qualified registered professional engineer sets the minimum clearance [29cfr1926.1410(c)(1)]; subpart V work uses employer-established § 1926.960(c)(1)(i) distances [29cfr1926.1410(c)(2)].

Planned procedures [29cfr1926.1410(d)] include disabling automatic reclosing before work, if design permits [29cfr1926.1410(d)(1)]; a continuously connected, well-positioned spotter with a visual aid, giving timely information, with direct communication equipment where necessary [29cfr1926.1410(d)(2)]; and a flagged or similarly marked elevated warning line or barricade, unattached to the crane and visible to you directly or by video [29cfr1926.1410(d)(3)]. An insulating link goes between the load line end (or below) and load [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(i)]. Subpart V is excepted from both. Link substitutes ran only until November 8, 2011 [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(iv)] and November 8, 2013 [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(v)].

Rigging that may enter the Table A distance, and any tag line, must be nonconductive [29cfr1926.1410(d)(5)] [29cfr1926.1410(d)(7)]. Any range limiter must be used and set to protect the established clearance [29cfr1926.1410(d)(6)]. Perimeter barricades are at least 10 feet out, or as far as feasible where obstructed [29cfr1926.1410(d)(8)]. Others may not touch the crane or the load line above the link; remote ground operators need isolating wireless controls or insulating mats [29cfr1926.1410(d)(9)]. Only essential personnel stay near [29cfr1926.1410(d)(10)]. Ground the equipment [29cfr1926.1410(d)(11)]. The utility installs line hose or cover-up unless unavailable for the voltage [29cfr1926.1410(d)(12)].

Procedures are documented, reviewed and implemented [29cfr1926.1410(e)] [29cfr1926.1410(f)] [29cfr1926.1410(g)]. One director has stop-work authority [29cfr1926.1410(h)]. Problems or inadequacy require safely stopping; before resuming, develop new procedures or have the utility deenergize and visibly ground, or relocate, the line [29cfr1926.1410(j)]. Safety devices and aids follow manufacturer conditions [29cfr1926.1410(k)]. Training follows § 1926.1408(g) [29cfr1926.1410(m)]. “§ 1926.1410 Power line safety (all voltages)—equipment operations closer than the Table A zone. Equipment operations in which any part of the equipment, load line, or load (including rigging and lifting accessories) is closer than the minimum approach distance under Table A of § 1926.1408 to an energized power line is prohibited, except where the employer demonstrates that all of the following requirements are met: (a) The employer determines that it is infeasible to do the work without breaching the minimum approach distance under Table A of § 1926.1408.”

§1926.1435(e)(5)(ii) Boom hoist limiting device “(ii) Boom hoist limiting device. The range of the boom must be limited at the minimum and maximum radius. Temporary alternative measures: Clearly mark the cable (so it can be seen by the operator) at a point that will give the operator sufficient time to stop the boom hoist within the minimum and maximum boom radius, or use a spotter who is in direct communication with the operator to inform the operator when this point is reached.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “With regard to tower cranes, “erecting and climbing” replaces the term “assembly,” and “dismantling” replaces the term “disassembly.” Regardless of whether the crane is initially erected to its full height or is climbed in stages, the process of increasing the height of the crane is an erection process. Assist crane means a crane used to assist in assembling or disassembling a crane. Attachments means any device that expands the range of tasks that can be done by the equipment. Examples include, but are not limited to: An auger, drill, magnet, pile-driver, and boom-attached personnel platform.”

This paragraph does not apply to the inspection of rails, rail stops, rail clamps and supporting surfaces when the railroad tracks are part of the general railroad system of transportation that is regulated pursuant to the Federal Railroad Administration under 49 CFR part 213.” §1926.1412 Inspections Each shift, a competent person begins a visual inspection beforehand and completes it before or during the shift. It covers at least the listed controls, drives, lines, hydraulic fluid, hooks, rope and reeving, electrical apparatus, tires, ground, level, windows, rail components and safety devices/aids. Disassembly or booming down is needed only if visual inspection or trial operation shows it. Determinations are reassessed during operation [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)]. Level is checked against manufacturer tolerances before each shift and after each move and setup [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(xi)]. Ground and rail items have exceptions for certain FRA-regulated track [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(x)] [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(xiii)]. Hazardous deficiencies under items (i)-(xiii), or additional type-specific items, take equipment out of service until corrected [29cfr1926.1412(d)(2)]. Safety device/aid deficiencies require §§ 1926.1415 and 1926.1416 action before use [29cfr1926.1412(d)(3)].

Monthly, while in service, the shift inspection applies. Use waits until it shows no corrective action is required [29cfr1926.1412(e)(2)]. The inspecting employer documents it [29cfr1926.1412(e)(3)(i)] and retains it at least three months [29cfr1926.1412(e)(3)(ii)].

Qualified persons inspect safety- or capacity-affecting modifications [29cfr1926.1412(a)(1)], safety-related repairs/adjustments [29cfr1926.1412(b)(1)] and completed assemblies [29cfr1926.1412(c)(1)]. Required criteria must be shown met before use [29cfr1926.1412(a)(2)] [29cfr1926.1412(b)(4)] [29cfr1926.1412(c)(3)].

At least every 12 months, qualified persons conduct the shift-based [29cfr1926.1412(f)(1)] and comprehensive inspections, disassembling as necessary [29cfr1926.1412(f)(2)], with functional testing [29cfr1926.1412(f)(3)]. Hazards remove equipment from service until corrected, subject to specified temporary alternative measures [29cfr1926.1412(f)(5)]. Deficiencies needing monitoring must be checked monthly [29cfr1926.1412(f)(6)]. Records are retained at least 12 months [29cfr1926.1412(f)(7)].

Severe service requires stopping use and inspection [29cfr1926.1412(g)]. Equipment idle 3 months or more needs a qualified person's monthly inspection before use [29cfr1926.1412(h)]. Specified stricter manufacturer procedures apply [29cfr1926.1412(j)]. “(xii) Operator cab windows for significant cracks, breaks, or other deficiencies that would hamper the operator's view. §1926.1412 Inspections

Each shift, a competent person begins a visual inspection beforehand and completes it before or during the shift. It covers at least the listed controls, drives, lines, hydraulic fluid, hooks, rope and reeving, electrical apparatus, tires, ground, level, windows, rail components and safety devices/aids. Disassembly or booming down is needed only if visual inspection or trial operation shows it. Determinations are reassessed during operation [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)]. Level is checked against manufacturer tolerances before each shift and after each move and setup [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(xi)]. Ground and rail items have exceptions for certain FRA-regulated track [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(x)] [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(xiii)]. Hazardous deficiencies under items (i)-(xiii), or additional type-specific items, take equipment out of service until corrected [29cfr1926.1412(d)(2)]. Safety device/aid deficiencies require §§ 1926.1415 and 1926.1416 action before use [29cfr1926.1412(d)(3)].

Monthly, while in service, the shift inspection applies. Use waits until it shows no corrective action is required [29cfr1926.1412(e)(2)]. The inspecting employer documents it [29cfr1926.1412(e)(3)(i)] and retains it at least three months [29cfr1926.1412(e)(3)(ii)].

Qualified persons inspect safety- or capacity-affecting modifications [29cfr1926.1412(a)(1)], safety-related repairs/adjustments [29cfr1926.1412(b)(1)] and completed assemblies [29cfr1926.1412(c)(1)]. Required criteria must be shown met before use [29cfr1926.1412(a)(2)] [29cfr1926.1412(b)(4)] [29cfr1926.1412(c)(3)].

At least every 12 months, qualified persons conduct the shift-based [29cfr1926.1412(f)(1)] and comprehensive inspections, disassembling as necessary [29cfr1926.1412(f)(2)], with functional testing [29cfr1926.1412(f)(3)]. Hazards remove equipment from service until corrected, subject to specified temporary alternative measures [29cfr1926.1412(f)(5)]. Deficiencies needing monitoring must be checked monthly [29cfr1926.1412(f)(6)]. Records are retained at least 12 months [29cfr1926.1412(f)(7)].

Severe service requires stopping use and inspection [29cfr1926.1412(g)]. Equipment idle 3 months or more needs a qualified person's monthly inspection before use [29cfr1926.1412(h)]. Specified stricter manufacturer procedures apply [29cfr1926.1412(j)].

(xii) Operator cab windows for significant cracks, breaks, or other deficiencies that would hamper the operator's view. (xiii) Rails, rail stops, rail clamps and supporting surfaces when the equipment has rail traveling. This paragraph does not apply to the inspection of rails, rail stops, rail clamps and supporting surfaces when the railroad tracks are part of the general railroad system of transportation that is regulated pursuant to the Federal Railroad Administration under 49 CFR part 213.

"Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Boom (tower cranes): On tower cranes, if the “boom” (i.e., principal horizontal structure) is fixed, it is referred to as a jib; if it is moveable up and down, it is referred to as a boom. Boom angle indicator means a device which measures the angle of the boom relative to horizontal. Boom hoist limiting device includes boom hoist disengaging device, boom hoist shut-off, boom hoist disconnect, boom hoist hydraulic relief, boom hoist kick-outs, automatic boom stop device, or derricking limiter.” §1926.1416(d)(1)(i)(B) “(B) Clearly mark the boom hoist cable (so that it can easily be seen by the operator) at a point that will give the operator sufficient time to stop the hoist to keep the boom within the minimum allowable radius. §1926.1417(h) Storm warning “(h) Storm warning. When a local storm warning has been issued, the competent person must determine whether it is necessary to implement manufacturer recommendations for securing the equipment.” §1926.1424 Work area control Swing radius requirements in (a)(2) apply to accessible areas where the rotating superstructure, permanent or temporary, poses a reasonably foreseeable risk of striking and injuring an employee, or pinching or crushing one against the equipment or another object [29cfr1926.1424(a)(1)].

To keep employees out, the employer must train "authorized personnel", meaning each employee assigned to work on or near the equipment, to recognize these hazard areas [29cfr1926.1424(a)(2)(i)]. The employer must also erect and maintain control lines, warning lines, railings or similar barriers at the boundaries. An exception applies when the employer can demonstrate that barriers are feasible neither on the ground nor on the equipment. Warning signs plus high visibility equipment markings must then clearly mark the areas, and employees must be trained on what these markings signify [29cfr1926.1424(a)(2)(ii)].

An employee heading to a hazard area location out of your view must ensure, personally or through someone they instruct, that you are informed beforehand [29cfr1926.1424(a)(3)(i)]. When you know an employee went to a location covered by (a)(1), you must not rotate the superstructure until informed, through a pre-arranged communication system, that the employee is "in a safe position" [29cfr1926.1424(a)(3)(ii)].

Where any part of a crane or derrick is within another's working radius, operations must be coordinated through an instituted system [29cfr1926.1424(b)]. “(i) Striking and injuring an employee; or (ii) Pinching/crushing an employee against another part of the equipment or another object. (2) To prevent employees from entering these hazard areas, the employer must: (i) Train each employee assigned to work on or near the equipment (“authorized personnel”) in how to recognize struck-by and pinch/crush hazard areas posed by the rotating superstructure. (ii) Erect and maintain control lines, warning lines, railings or similar barriers to mark the boundaries of the hazard areas.”

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. While you are not moving a suspended load, employees must be out of the fall zone unless they are hooking, unhooking or guiding it, making its initial attachment to a component or structure, or operating a concrete hopper or bucket [29cfr1926.1425(b)].

§1926.1419(c)(1) “(1) When using hand signals, the Standard Method must be used (see appendix A of this subpart). Exception: Where use of the Standard Method for hand signals is infeasible, or where an operation or use of an attachment is not covered in the Standard Method, non-standard hand signals may be used in accordance with paragraph (c)(2) of this section.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Stability (flotation device) means the tendency of a barge, pontoons, vessel or other means of flotation to return to an upright position after having been inclined by an external force. Standard Method means the protocol in appendix A of this subpart for hand signals. Such as means “such as, but not limited to.” Superstructure: See Upperworks. Tagline means a rope (usually fiber) attached to a lifted load for purposes of controlling load spinning and pendular motions or used to stabilize a bucket or magnet during material handling operations.” §1926.1419 Signals—general requirements Provide a signal person if the point of operation is not in your full view, the view in the travel direction is obstructed, or you or the load handler find one necessary for site-specific safety concerns [29cfr1926.1419(a)]. Signals must be hand, voice, audible or new [29cfr1926.1419(b)], and they and their means of transmission must suit site conditions [29cfr1926.1419(e)]. New signals require an employer demonstration [29cfr1926.1419(d)].

Use Standard Method hand signals unless that is infeasible or it does not cover the operation or attachment use [29cfr1926.1419(c)(1)]. Before using non-standard signals, the signal person, operator and any lift director must make contact and agree on them [29cfr1926.1419(c)(2)].

Safely stop operations requiring signals if transmission is interrupted. Wait until it is restored and a proper signal is given and understood [29cfr1926.1419(f)]. If you need to communicate a safety problem to the signal person, stop safely; resume only after you both agree it is resolved [29cfr1926.1419(g)].

Only one person signals at a time, subject to the paragraph (j) exception [29cfr1926.1419(h)]: anyone aware of a safety problem must alert you or the signal person with a stop or emergency stop signal [29cfr1926.1419(j)]. §1926.1421(a) “(a) Prior to beginning operations, the operator, signal person and lift director (if there is one), must contact each other and agree on the voice signals that will be used. Once the voice signals are agreed upon, these workers need not meet again to discuss voice signals unless another worker is added or substituted, there is confusion about the voice signals, or a voice signal is to be changed.” §1926.1421 Signals—voice signals—additional requirements Before operations begin, you, the signal person and the lift director (if there is one) must contact each other and agree on the voice signals to be used [29cfr1926.1421(a)]. Once you have agreed, another meeting about voice signals is not needed unless one of these occurs: another worker is added or substituted, there is confusion about the voice signals, or a voice signal is to be changed [29cfr1926.1421(a)].

Each voice signal must contain three elements in a set order [29cfr1926.1421(b)]. The text lists them as "function (such as hoist, boom, etc.), direction; distance and/or speed; function, stop command." Following the semicolon grouping, a signal starts with the function and its direction. It then gives the distance and/or speed. It finishes with the function and the stop command [29cfr1926.1421(b)]. Hoist and boom appear as examples of functions, and the "etc." shows that the examples are not a complete list.

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Articulating crane means a crane whose boom consists of a series of folding, pin connected structural members, typically manipulated to extend or retract by power from hydraulic cylinders. Assembly/Disassembly means the assembly and/or disassembly of equipment covered under this standard. With regard to tower cranes, “erecting and climbing” replaces the term “assembly,” and “dismantling” replaces the term “disassembly.” Regardless of whether the crane is initially erected to its full height or is climbed in stages, the process of increasing the height of the crane is an erection process.”

§1926.1424 Work area control Swing radius requirements in (a)(2) apply to accessible areas where the rotating superstructure, permanent or temporary, poses a reasonably foreseeable risk of striking and injuring an employee, or pinching or crushing one against the equipment or another object [29cfr1926.1424(a)(1)].

To keep employees out, the employer must train "authorized personnel", meaning each employee assigned to work on or near the equipment, to recognize these hazard areas [29cfr1926.1424(a)(2)(i)]. The employer must also erect and maintain control lines, warning lines, railings or similar barriers at the boundaries. An exception applies when the employer can demonstrate that barriers are feasible neither on the ground nor on the equipment. Warning signs plus high visibility equipment markings must then clearly mark the areas, and employees must be trained on what these markings signify [29cfr1926.1424(a)(2)(ii)].

An employee heading to a hazard area location out of your view must ensure, personally or through someone they instruct, that you are informed beforehand [29cfr1926.1424(a)(3)(i)]. When you know an employee went to a location covered by (a)(1), you must not rotate the superstructure until informed, through a pre-arranged communication system, that the employee is "in a safe position" [29cfr1926.1424(a)(3)(ii)].

Where any part of a crane or derrick is within another's working radius, operations must be coordinated through an instituted system [29cfr1926.1424(b)]. “§ 1926.1424 Work area control. (a) Swing radius hazards.”

§1926.1428(c)(3) “(3) Have a basic understanding of equipment operation and limitations, including the crane dynamics involved in swinging and stopping loads and boom deflection from hoisting loads.” §1926.1419 Signals—general requirements Provide a signal person if the point of operation is not in your full view, the view in the travel direction is obstructed, or you or the load handler find one necessary for site-specific safety concerns [29cfr1926.1419(a)]. Signals must be hand, voice, audible or new [29cfr1926.1419(b)], and they and their means of transmission must suit site conditions [29cfr1926.1419(e)]. New signals require an employer demonstration [29cfr1926.1419(d)].

Use Standard Method hand signals unless that is infeasible or it does not cover the operation or attachment use [29cfr1926.1419(c)(1)]. Before using non-standard signals, the signal person, operator and any lift director must make contact and agree on them [29cfr1926.1419(c)(2)].

Safely stop operations requiring signals if transmission is interrupted. Wait until it is restored and a proper signal is given and understood [29cfr1926.1419(f)]. If you need to communicate a safety problem to the signal person, stop safely; resume only after you both agree it is resolved [29cfr1926.1419(g)].

§1926.1427 Operator training, certification, and evaluation Covered equipment requires training, certification or licensing, and evaluation; otherwise, you operate only as a supervised trainee [29cfr1926.1427(a)(1)]. Derricks, sidebooms and equipment rated 2,000 pounds or less are excepted, but their training rules remain [29cfr1926.1427(a)(2)]. Military qualifications are employer-specific and last as the issuer stipulates [29cfr1926.1427(a)(3)].

Trainees need formal and practical instruction, assigned tasks within their ability, and continuous on-site monitoring by a qualified employer employee or agent doing nothing distracting [29cfr1926.1427(b)]. Non-tower cranes require line of sight plus verbal or hand signals; tower cranes require direct communication. Breaks are limited to 15 minutes, one per hour, after a task-and-limits briefing, with tasks within ability [29cfr1926.1427(b)(4)]. Uncertified trainees cannot work where equipment, line or load at maximum radius could reach within 20 feet of power lines up to 350 kV, or 50 feet above that voltage. They also cannot hoist personnel, make multiple-equipment lifts, or work over shafts or cofferdams or in tank farms. Multiple-lift rigging is barred unless the trainer finds their skills sufficient [29cfr1926.1427(b)(3)].

Qualifying state or local licensing governs within its jurisdiction (maximum validity 5 years); otherwise certification is required, with no employee cost [29cfr1926.1427(c)]. Accredited certification is type-based or type-and-capacity-based, portable among employers required to use that option, and valid 5 years; accreditation review occurs at least every 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(d)]. Audited-employer certification lasts 5 years and is not portable [29cfr1926.1427(e)(6)]. Audits occur within 3 months of program start, then at least every 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(e)(3)]. Significant deficiencies halt qualification until confirmed correction, require re-audit within 180 days afterward and an auditor's OSHA report within 15 days of determination; auditors keep audit records 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(e)(5)].

Evaluation covers safe operation, equipment-specific features and assigned hoisting [29cfr1926.1427(f)(1)]. Other equipment is allowed if the employer can demonstrate no substantially different abilities are needed [29cfr1926.1427(f)(5)]. Performance or knowledge evaluation indicating a need triggers retraining and subject re-evaluation [29cfr1926.1427(b)(5)] [29cfr1926.1427(f)(7)]. Pre-December 10, 2018 employees may be covered by prior assessments [29cfr1926.1427(f)(2)]. The section's effective date is December 10, 2018; evaluation and documentation, February 7, 2019 [29cfr1926.1427(k)]. “However, except as provided in paragraph (b)(3)(v) of this section, the operator-in-training shall not operate the equipment in any of the following circumstances unless certified in accordance with paragraph (c) of this section: (i) If any part of the equipment, load line, or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), if operated up to the equipment's maximum working radius in the work zone (see § 1926.1408(a)(1)), could get within 20 feet of a power line that is up to 350 kV, or within 50 feet of a power line that is over 350 kV.” §1926.1411 Power line safety—while traveling under or near power lines with no load These procedures and criteria cover equipment traveling with no load under or near a power line on a construction site. Loaded travel falls under § 1926.1408, § 1926.1409 or § 1926.1410, whichever is appropriate, and § 1926.1417(u) [29cfr1926.1411(a)].

The employer must ensure the boom/mast and its support system are lowered sufficiently [29cfr1926.1411(b)(1)], Table T clearances are maintained [29cfr1926.1411(b)(2)], and speed and terrain effects, including boom/mast movement, are considered so they do not cause a breach of minimum clearance [29cfr1926.1411(b)(3)].

Table T minimums, by nominal AC voltage in kV, are: up to 0.75, 4 feet; over .75 to 50, 6 feet; over 50 to 345, 10 feet; over 345 to 750, 16 feet; over 750 to 1,000, 20 feet. Over 1,000, the distance is established by the utility owner/operator or a registered professional engineer qualified in electrical power transmission and distribution [29cfr1926.1411-table-T].

If any part of traveling equipment will get closer than 20 feet to the line, a dedicated spotter in continuous contact with you is required [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)]. The spotter must be positioned to gauge clearance effectively, use direct communication equipment where necessary, and give you "timely information" so clearance can be maintained [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)].

At night or in poor visibility, lines must also be illuminated or otherwise located, and a safe travel path identified and used [29cfr1926.1411(b)(5)]. “(2) The clearances specified in Table T of this section are maintained. (3) The effects of speed and terrain on equipment movement (including movement of the boom/mast) are considered so that those effects do not cause the minimum clearance distances specified in Table T of this section to be breached. (4) Dedicated spotter. If any part of the equipment while traveling will get closer than 20 feet to the power line, the employer must ensure that a dedicated spotter who is in continuous contact with the driver/operator is used.” §1926.1408 Power line safety (up to 350 kV)—equipment operations Before operating, the employer must identify the work zone: demarcated boundaries you are prohibited from passing, or 360 degrees out to maximum working radius [29cfr1926.1408(a)(1)]. If equipment, load line or load (with rigging and accessories) could get within 20 feet of a line at that radius, one option applies: utility-confirmed deenergizing with visible worksite grounding, 20-foot clearance, or Table A clearance [29cfr1926.1408(a)(2)]. Table A (AC, nominal kV): up to 50, 10 feet; over 50 to 200, 15; over 200 to 350, 20; over 350 to 500, 25; over 500 to 750, 35; over 750 to 1,000, 45; over 1,000, set by the utility or a qualified registered professional engineer. Upper values are inclusive [29cfr1926.1408-table-A]. Requested voltage information is due from the utility within two working days [29cfr1926.1408(c)].

Where encroachment precautions are required, there must be a planning meeting, non-conductive tag lines if used, and a flagged or high-visibility warning line, barricade or sign line in your view at the applicable distance [29cfr1926.1408(b)]. At least one measure is also required: proximity alarm, dedicated spotter, automatic warning device, automatic range limiter, or insulating link/device; subpart V work is excepted from this [29cfr1926.1408(b)(4)] [29cfr1926.1408(b)(5)]. If you cannot see the warning line, a dedicated spotter is required plus one of the other four [29cfr1926.1408(b)(3)]. Spotters need continuous contact, a visual aid, effective positioning, direct communication equipment where necessary, and must give timely information [29cfr1926.1408(b)(4)(ii)].

Operating below lines requires confirmed deenergizing and worksite grounding unless an exception applies [29cfr1926.1408(d)]. Presume lines energized [29cfr1926.1408(e)]. Near transmitter towers where charge could be induced, deenergize the transmitter, or ground the equipment and use only non-conductive tag lines if any [29cfr1926.1408(f)]. Training covers contact procedures, line presumptions, device limitations and grounding [29cfr1926.1408(g)(1)]. Safety devices, aids and contact-prevention means used for compliance must meet manufacturer procedures and conditions [29cfr1926.1408(h)]. “§ 1926.1408 Power line safety (up to 350 kV)—equipment operations. (a) Hazard assessments and precautions inside the work zone. Before beginning equipment operations, the employer must: (1) Identify the work zone by either: (i) Demarcating boundaries (such as with flags, or a device such as a range limit device or range control warning device) and prohibiting the operator from operating the equipment past those boundaries, or (ii) Defining the work zone as the area 360 degrees around the equipment, up to the equipment's maximum working radius.”

Before operating, the employer must identify the work zone: demarcated boundaries you are prohibited from passing, or 360 degrees out to maximum working radius [29cfr1926.1408(a)(1)].

body.text: §1926.1427 Operator training, certification, and evaluation

Covered equipment requires training, certification or licensing, and evaluation; otherwise, you operate only as a supervised trainee [29cfr1926.1427(a)(1)]. Derricks, sidebooms and equipment rated 2,000 pounds or less are excepted, but their training rules remain [29cfr1926.1427(a)(2)]. Military qualifications are employer-specific and last as the issuer stipulates [29cfr1926.1427(a)(3)].

Trainees need formal and practical instruction, assigned tasks within their ability, and continuous on-site monitoring by a qualified employer employee or agent doing nothing distracting [29cfr1926.1427(b)]. Non-tower cranes require line of sight plus verbal or hand signals; tower cranes require direct communication. Breaks are limited to 15 minutes, one per hour, after a task-and-limits briefing, with tasks within ability [29cfr1926.1427(b)(4)]. Uncertified trainees cannot work where equipment, line or load at maximum radius could reach within 20 feet of power lines up to 350 kV, or 50 feet above that voltage. They also cannot hoist personnel, make multiple-equipment lifts, or work over shafts or cofferdams or in tank farms. Multiple-lift rigging is barred unless the trainer finds their skills sufficient [29cfr1926.1427(b)(3)].

Qualifying state or local licensing governs within its jurisdiction (maximum validity 5 years); otherwise certification is required, with no employee cost [29cfr1926.1427(c)]. Accredited certification is type-based or type-and-capacity-based, portable among employers required to use that option, and valid 5 years; accreditation review occurs at least every 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(d)]. Audited-employer certification lasts 5 years and is not portable [29cfr1926.1427(e)(6)]. Audits occur within 3 months of program start, then at least every 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(e)(3)]. Significant deficiencies halt qualification until confirmed correction, require re-audit within 180 days afterward and an auditor's OSHA report within 15 days of determination; auditors keep audit records 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(e)(5)].

Evaluation covers safe operation, equipment-specific features and assigned hoisting [29cfr1926.1427(f)(1)]. Other equipment is allowed if the employer can demonstrate no substantially different abilities are needed [29cfr1926.1427(f)(5)]. Performance or knowledge evaluation indicating a need triggers retraining and subject re-evaluation [29cfr1926.1427(b)(5)] [29cfr1926.1427(f)(7)]. Pre-December 10, 2018 employees may be covered by prior assessments [29cfr1926.1427(f)(2)]. The section's effective date is December 10, 2018; evaluation and documentation, February 7, 2019 [29cfr1926.1427(k)].

However, except as provided in paragraph (b)(3)(v) of this section, the operator-in-training shall not operate the equipment in any of the following circumstances unless certified in accordance with paragraph (c) of this section: (i) If any part of the equipment, load line, or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), if operated up to the equipment's maximum working radius in the work zone (see § 1926.1408(a)(1)), could get within 20 feet of a power line that is up to 350 kV, or within 50 feet of a power line that is over 350 kV.
