§1926.1423(c)(4) “(4) Tower cranes manufactured after November 8, 2011 must be equipped so as to provide safe access and egress between the ground and the cab, machinery platforms, and tower (mast), by the provision of devices such as steps, handholds, ladders, and guardrails/railings/grabrails.” §1926.1423(c)(4)(i) “(i) Steps, handholds, ladders, and guardrails/railings/grabrails must meet the criteria of ISO 11660-1:2008(E) (incorporated by reference, see § 1926.6) and ISO 11660-3:2008(E) (incorporated by reference, see § 1926.6) or SAE J185 (May 2003) (incorporated by reference, see § 1926.6) except where infeasible.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “See Upperworks. Tagline means a rope (usually fiber) attached to a lifted load for purposes of controlling load spinning and pendular motions or used to stabilize a bucket or magnet during material handling operations. Tender means an individual responsible for monitoring and communicating with a diver. Tilt up or tilt down operation means raising/lowering a load from the horizontal to vertical or vertical to horizontal. Tower crane is a type of lifting structure which utilizes a vertical mast or tower to support a working boom (jib) in an elevated position.”

§1926.1430(c)(3)(i) “(i) On friction equipment, whenever moving a boom off a support, first raise the boom a short distance (sufficient to take the load of the boom) to determine if the boom hoist brake needs to be adjusted. On other types of equipment with a boom, the same practice is applicable, except that typically there is no means of adjusting the brake; if the brake does not hold, a repair is necessary. See § 1926.1417(f) and (j) for additional requirements.” §1926.1430 Training Your employer must train you on safe operation of the equipment you will use, in accordance with § 1926.1427(a) and (b) [29cfr1926.1430(c)(1)]. Operators covered under the exception in § 1926.1427(a)(2) must also be trained on safe operation of their equipment [29cfr1926.1430(c)(2)].

Operators of equipment covered by this subpart are trained in specific practices [29cfr1926.1430(c)(3)]. On friction equipment, whenever moving a boom off a support, you "first raise the boom a short distance", enough to take the boom's load, to determine whether the boom hoist brake needs adjustment. The practice also applies to other equipment with a boom. There, typically the brake can't be adjusted, so if it doesn't hold, "a repair is necessary". See also § 1926.1417(f) and (j) [29cfr1926.1430(c)(3)(i)]. Where available, training covers the manufacturer's emergency procedures for halting unintended equipment movement [29cfr1926.1430(c)(3)(ii)].

You also receive training in the tag-out and start-up procedures in § 1926.1417(f) and (g), as do other employees authorized to start or energize equipment or operate controls [29cfr1926.1430(f)]. Employees working with the equipment are trained on holes, crush/pinch points and § 1926.1424 hazards [29cfr1926.1430(e)].

Employers must evaluate required trainees to confirm understanding [29cfr1926.1430(g)(1)], give refresher training when conduct or a knowledge evaluation indicates retraining is necessary [29cfr1926.1430(g)(2)], and provide subpart CC training free to employees [29cfr1926.1430(g)(3)]. Other paragraphs address powerlines, signal persons, and competent and qualified persons [29cfr1926.1430(a)] [29cfr1926.1430(b)] [29cfr1926.1430(d)]. “(2) The employer must train each operator covered under the exception of § 1926.1427(a)(2) on the safe operation of the equipment the operator will be using. (3) The employer must train each operator of the equipment covered by this subpart in the following practices: (i) On friction equipment, whenever moving a boom off a support, first raise the boom a short distance (sufficient to take the load of the boom) to determine if the boom hoist brake needs to be adjusted.” §1926.1426(b)(1)(ii) “(ii) A secondary braking or locking device, which is manually or automatically engaged, to back-up the primary brake while the boom is held (such as a secondary friction brake or a ratchet and pawl device).”

§1926.1424(a)(2)(i) “(i) Train each employee assigned to work on or near the equipment (“authorized personnel”) in how to recognize struck-by and pinch/crush hazard areas posed by the rotating superstructure.” §1926.1424(a)(2) “(ii) Erect and maintain control lines, warning lines, railings or similar barriers to mark the boundaries of the hazard areas. Exception: When the employer can demonstrate that it is neither feasible to erect such barriers on the ground nor on the equipment, the hazard areas must be clearly marked by a combination of warning signs (such as “Danger—Swing/Crush Zone”) and high visibility markings on the equipment that identify the hazard areas. In addition, the employer must train each employee to understand what these markings signify.” §1926.1427 Operator training, certification, and evaluation Covered equipment requires training, certification or licensing, and evaluation; otherwise, you operate only as a supervised trainee [29cfr1926.1427(a)(1)]. Derricks, sidebooms and equipment rated 2,000 pounds or less are excepted, but their training rules remain [29cfr1926.1427(a)(2)]. Military qualifications are employer-specific and last as the issuer stipulates [29cfr1926.1427(a)(3)].

Trainees need formal and practical instruction, assigned tasks within their ability, and continuous on-site monitoring by a qualified employer employee or agent doing nothing distracting [29cfr1926.1427(b)]. Non-tower cranes require line of sight plus verbal or hand signals; tower cranes require direct communication. Breaks are limited to 15 minutes, one per hour, after a task-and-limits briefing, with tasks within ability [29cfr1926.1427(b)(4)]. Uncertified trainees cannot work where equipment, line or load at maximum radius could reach within 20 feet of power lines up to 350 kV, or 50 feet above that voltage. They also cannot hoist personnel, make multiple-equipment lifts, or work over shafts or cofferdams or in tank farms. Multiple-lift rigging is barred unless the trainer finds their skills sufficient [29cfr1926.1427(b)(3)].

Qualifying state or local licensing governs within its jurisdiction (maximum validity 5 years); otherwise certification is required, with no employee cost [29cfr1926.1427(c)]. Accredited certification is type-based or type-and-capacity-based, portable among employers required to use that option, and valid 5 years; accreditation review occurs at least every 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(d)]. Audited-employer certification lasts 5 years and is not portable [29cfr1926.1427(e)(6)]. Audits occur within 3 months of program start, then at least every 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(e)(3)]. Significant deficiencies halt qualification until confirmed correction, require re-audit within 180 days afterward and an auditor's OSHA report within 15 days of determination; auditors keep audit records 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(e)(5)].

Evaluation covers safe operation, equipment-specific features and assigned hoisting [29cfr1926.1427(f)(1)]. Other equipment is allowed if the employer can demonstrate no substantially different abilities are needed [29cfr1926.1427(f)(5)]. Performance or knowledge evaluation indicating a need triggers retraining and subject re-evaluation [29cfr1926.1427(b)(5)] [29cfr1926.1427(f)(7)]. Pre-December 10, 2018 employees may be covered by prior assessments [29cfr1926.1427(f)(2)]. The section's effective date is December 10, 2018; evaluation and documentation, February 7, 2019 [29cfr1926.1427(k)]. “(v) For the purposes of compliance with this section, a license is valid for the period of time stipulated by the licensing department/office, but no longer than 5 years. (2) Certification. When an operator is not required to be licensed under paragraph (c)(1) of this section, the operator must be certified in accordance with paragraph (d) or (e) of this section. (3) No cost to employees. Whenever operator certification/licensure is required under this section, the employer must provide the certification/licensure at no cost to employees. (4) Provision of testing and training.”

Appendix C to Subpart CC of Part 1926 (a)(4)(iii) “(iii) Insulated links.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Hoist means a mechanical device for lifting and lowering loads by winding a line onto or off a drum. Hoisting is the act of raising, lowering or otherwise moving a load in the air with equipment covered by this standard. As used in this standard, “hoisting” can be done by means other than wire rope/hoist drum equipment. Include/including means “including, but not limited to.” Insulating link/device means an insulating device listed, labeled, or accepted by a Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory in accordance with 29 CFR 1910.7.” §1926.1410(d)(4) Insulating link/device “(v) Until November 8, 2013, the following procedure may be substituted for the requirement in (d)(4)(i) of this section: (A) The employer must use a link/device manufactured on or before November 8, 2011, that meets the definition of an insulating link/device, except that it has not been approved by a Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory, and that is maintained and used in accordance with manufacturer requirements and recommendations, and is installed at a point between the end of the load line (or below) and the load;”

§1926.1431(k)(11)(ii) Factory-produced boom-mounted personnel platforms that incorporate a winch as original equipment “(ii) Factory-produced boom-mounted personnel platforms that incorporate a winch as original equipment. Loads are permitted to be hoisted by such a winch while employees occupy the personnel platform only where the load on the winch line does not exceed 500 pounds and does not exceed the rated capacity of the winch and platform.” Appendix B to Subpart CC of Part 1926 Appendix B to Subpart CC of Part 1926—Assembly/Disassembly: Sample Procedures for Minimizing the Risk of Unintended Dangerous Boom Movement For pin removal, the appendix cites § 1926.1404(f)(1): employees must not be under the boom, jib, or other components unless § 1926.1404(f)(2) is met. That exception applies when the employer demonstrates that site constraints require one or more employees to be there. The A/D director must then implement procedures that "minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement and minimize the duration and extent of exposure under the boom" [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

In the sample, aboveground piping prevents lowering the boom, and the aerial lift, based on the near side, cannot be repositioned, so its basket must go under the boom. A rigged assist crane supports the detaching section, with particular care that the end near the pin removers is well supported. Far side pins come out first, the basket returns to the near side as soon as possible, then near side pins come out [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

During assembly/disassembly, the load's center of gravity must be identified if the stability method requires it. With insufficient information, measures must prevent unintended dangerous movement from misidentifying it. In the sample, the director cannot determine the pick point above a non-symmetrical top section's center of gravity. With personnel clear, it is raised a few inches to check for tipping. If it tips, the hoist line is repositioned and the test repeated until the director determines it can be moved without dangerous movement [29cfr1926.cc.appB]. “A boom cannot be disassembled on the ground because of aboveground piping (as might be found, for example, in an oil refinery) that precludes lowering the boom to the ground. The boom must therefore be disassembled in the air, and the employees who remove the pins must perform that work from an aerial lift whose base is positioned on one side (the near side) of the boom. To gain access to the pins on the far side, the aerial lift basket must move under the boom, since, due to lack of room, the aerial lift cannot be repositioned on the far side.” §1926.1436(a) “all sections of this subpart apply to derricks unless specified otherwise. A derrick is powered equipment consisting of a mast or equivalent member that is held at or near the end by guys or braces, with or without a boom, and its hoisting mechanism. The mast/equivalent member and/or the load is moved by the hoisting mechanism (typically base-mounted) and operating ropes. Derricks include: A-frame, basket, breast, Chicago boom, gin pole (except gin poles used for erection of communication towers), guy, shearleg, stiffleg, and variations of such equipment.”

§1926.1432 Multiple-crane/derrick lifts—supplemental requirements These supplemental requirements apply to a crane/derrick operation in which more than one crane/derrick will be supporting the load. The operation must be planned before it begins [29cfr1926.1432(a)].

For the plan itself, a qualified person must develop it [29cfr1926.1432(a)(1)]. It must be designed "to ensure that the requirements of this subpart are met" [29cfr1926.1432(a)(2)]. A decision point concerns engineering: where the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure that it is provided [29cfr1926.1432(a)(3)].

For implementation, the lift must be directed by a lift director, and there are two acceptable arrangements [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. The first is a single person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person. The second is a competent person "who is assisted by one or more qualified persons" [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. Under the wording of that paragraph, a competent person who does not also meet the qualified person criteria needs that assistance to fit either arrangement.

The lift director must also review the plan in a meeting with all workers who will be involved with the operation [29cfr1926.1432(b)(2)]. “The planning must meet the following requirements: (1) The plan must be developed by a qualified person. (2) The plan must be designed to ensure that the requirements of this subpart are met. (3) Where the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure that it is provided. (b) Plan implementation. (1) The multiple-crane/derrick lift must be directed by a person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or by a competent person who is assisted by one or more qualified persons (lift director).” §1926.1432(b)(1) “(1) The multiple-crane/derrick lift must be directed by a person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or by a competent person who is assisted by one or more qualified persons (lift director).”

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Flange points are points of contact between rope and drum flange where the rope changes layers. Floating cranes/derricks means equipment designed by the manufacturer (or employer) for marine use by permanent attachment to a barge, pontoons, vessel or other means of flotation. For example means “one example, although there are others.” Free fall (of the load line) means that only the brake is used to regulate the descent of the load line (the drive mechanism is not used to drive the load down faster or retard its lowering).”

response.text:
§1926.1435(b)(5) Plumb tolerance “(5) Plumb tolerance. Towers must be erected plumb to the manufacturer's tolerance and verified by a qualified person. Where the manufacturer does not specify plumb tolerance, the crane tower must be plumb to a tolerance of at least 1:500 (approximately 1 inch in 40 feet).” §1926.1435 Tower cranes Subpart rules apply unless specified otherwise [29cfr1926.1435(a)], including §§1926.1403–.1406 for erecting, climbing and dismantling, except as otherwise specified [29cfr1926.1435(b)(1)]. Self-erecting cranes have an entry restriction until locked and cleared, with a manufacturer-instruction exception [29cfr1926.1435(b)(2)]. Foundations need manufacturer or registered professional engineer (RPE) design [29cfr1926.1435(b)(3)]. The A/D director addresses §1926.1404(h)(1)–(9), installation per design, backward stability and wind [29cfr1926.1435(b)(4)]. Plumb defaults to at least 1:500 (approximately 1 inch in 40 feet) absent a manufacturer tolerance; a qualified person verifies it [29cfr1926.1435(b)(5)]. Multiple hammerheads may overfly but not be able to contact another's structure [29cfr1926.1435(b)(6)]. Climbing [29cfr1926.1435(b)(7)], counterweight/ballast [29cfr1926.1435(b)(8)] and signs [29cfr1926.1435(c)] have manufacturer or RPE controls.

Safety devices cover stops, rail clamps, hydraulic protections, automatic-setting brakes, control levers and an emergency stop [29cfr1926.1435(d)(2)]. All must work before starting. On failure, stop safely; the crane leaves service until repair, without alternative measures [29cfr1926.1435(d)(3)]. For a failed operational aid, stop until temporary measures are in place or it works [29cfr1926.1435(e)(4)]. Follow any more protective manufacturer measures [29cfr1926.1435(e)(3)].

Category I covers travel, boom, two-block, drum, moment and line-pull limits plus boom-drum locking. Repair within 7 calendar days; if parts are documented as ordered within 7, repair within 7 of receipt [29cfr1926.1435(e)(5)]. Alternatives include marks, spotters, radius and load determination, capacity checks or manual setting. Trolley Option B and rail travel require communicating spotters within 10 feet of end stops. Post-November 8, 2011 cranes need protection for the last 2 drum wraps.

Category II covers angle/radius, deceleration, wind and load indicators. The limit is 30 days; with parts documented as ordered within 7 but arriving too late, 7 from receipt [29cfr1926.1435(e)(6)]. The post-November 8, 2011 condition applies to hammerhead radius and load indicators. Alternatives include measurements, cab notices, wind information or estimates, and load-weight determination.

Inspections include pre-erection, post-erection load testing, monthly and annual items [29cfr1926.1435(f)]. “In addition, the A/D director must address the following: (i) Foundations and structural supports. The A/D director must determine that tower crane foundations and structural supports are installed in accordance with their design. (ii) Loss of backward stability. Backward stability before swinging self erecting cranes or cranes on traveling or static undercarriages. (iii) Wind speed. Wind must not exceed the speed recommended by the manufacturer or, where manufacturer does not specify this information, the speed determined by a qualified person. (5) Plumb tolerance.”

The tower crane must be equipped with a device which automatically prevents damage from contact between the load block, overhaul ball, or similar component, and the boom tip (or fixed upper block or similar component).” §1926.1441(d)(2) Anti two-blocking “(2) Anti two-blocking. The employer must ensure that equipment covered by this section manufactured more than one year after November 8, 2010 have either an anti two-block device that meets the requirements of § 1926.1416(d)(3), or is designed so that, in the event of a two-block situation, no damage or load failure will occur (for example, by using a power unit that stalls in response to a two-block situation).” §1926.1431(d)(5)(v) Anti two-block “(v) Anti two-block. A device which automatically prevents damage and load failure from contact between the load block, overhaul ball, or similar component, and the boom tip (or fixed upper block or similar component) must be used. The device(s) must prevent such damage/failure at all points where two-blocking could occur. Exception: This device is not required when hoisting personnel in pile driving operations. Instead, paragraph (p)(2) of this section specifies how to prevent two-blocking during such operations.”

§1926.1401 Definitions

These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. §1910.180(d)(2) Regular inspection

(2) Regular inspection. Inspection procedure for cranes in regular service is divided into two general classifications based upon the intervals at which inspection should be performed. The intervals in turn are dependent upon the nature of the critical components of the crane and the degree of their exposure to wear, deterioration, or malfunction. The two general classifications are herein designated as “frequent” and “periodic”, with respective intervals between inspections as defined below: (i) Frequent inspection: Daily to monthly intervals.
(B) Those sections that are normally hidden during shift and monthly inspections.

§1926.1437(a) “(a) This section contains supplemental requirements for floating cranes/derricks and land cranes/derricks on barges, pontoons, vessels or other means of flotation (i.e., vessel/flotation device). The sections of this subpart apply to floating cranes/derricks and land cranes/derricks on barges, pontoons, vessels or other means of flotation, unless specified otherwise. The requirements of this section do not apply when using jacked barges when the jacks are deployed to the river, lake, or sea bed and the barge is fully supported by the jacks.” §1926.1437 Floating cranes/derricks and land cranes/derricks on barges This supplements the subpart for floating and barge-mounted cranes and derricks, excluding jacked barges fully supported by deployed jacks [29cfr1926.1437(a)]. Work area control applies except § 1926.1424(a)(2)(ii); use barriers, or signs plus equipment markings and employee training [29cfr1926.1437(c)]. § 1926.1425 doesn't apply [29cfr1926.1437(d)]. Add list/trim and house-lock devices, plus a wind indicator when a competent person finds wind relevant [29cfr1926.1437(e)]. Anti two-block applies only to personnel hoisting or hoisting over occupied cofferdams or shafts; listed work has load-weighing relief [29cfr1926.1437(f)]. Cab or no-cab information-access rules apply [29cfr1926.1437(g)].

Competent persons inspect the flotation each shift and monthly [29cfr1926.1437(h)(3)]. Annual external and four-year internal inspections require specified expertise; hazards remove the vessel from service, and flagged nonhazards are monitored [29cfr1926.1437(h)(4)] [29cfr1926.1437(h)(5)]. Document monthly, annual and four-year inspections; keep four-year records at least 4 years [29cfr1926.1437(h)(6)].

Diver work requires dedicated crane use until all divers return, continuous control attendance, tender sightline or electronic signals, and no-shift securing [29cfr1926.1437(j)]. Don't exceed vessel environmental, operating or transit limits [29cfr1926.1437(k)].

For permanent marine equipment, follow water charts and their parameters; charts consider minimum 40 mph wind [29cfr1926.1437(m)(1)]. List/trim maximums, in degrees, are 5 each at 25 tons or less, 7 over 25, and 10 for derricks [29cfr1926.1437-table-M1]. Stability: 60 mph with 2 ft freeboard at rated capacity or high boom/no load; 1 ft at capacity plus 25% [29cfr1926.1437-table-M2]; backward stability, high boom/no load/full back list, 90 mph [29cfr1926.1437-table-M3]. Employer-made equipment needs engineer-signed proof [29cfr1926.1437(m)(4)].

Land equipment needs expert derating [29cfr1926.1437(n)(2)]. Vessel list/trim cannot exceed the least of 5 degrees or the manufacturer's limit (qualified person's if unspecified), and must preserve above-water decks and a fully submerged bottom [29cfr1926.1437(n)(3)(i)] [29cfr1926.1437(n)(4)]. Crane list/trim limits also apply [29cfr1926.1437(n)(3)(ii)]. Secure by attachment, corral, rails or centerline cable, except qualifying mobile auxiliaries under a plan [29cfr1926.1437(n)]. Both equipment categories have hull requirements [29cfr1926.1437(m)(5)] [29cfr1926.1437(n)(7)]. “(a) This section contains supplemental requirements for floating cranes/derricks and land cranes/derricks on barges, pontoons, vessels or other means of flotation (i.e., vessel/flotation device). The sections of this subpart apply to floating cranes/derricks and land cranes/derricks on barges, pontoons, vessels or other means of flotation, unless specified otherwise. The requirements of this section do not apply when using jacked barges when the jacks are deployed to the river, lake, or sea bed and the barge is fully supported by the jacks.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Tilt up or tilt down operation means raising/lowering a load from the horizontal to vertical or vertical to horizontal. Tower crane is a type of lifting structure which utilizes a vertical mast or tower to support a working boom (jib) in an elevated position. Loads are suspended from the working boom. While the working boom may be of the fixed type (horizontal or angled) or have luffing capability, it can always rotate to swing loads, either by rotating on the top of the tower (top slewing) or by the rotation of the tower (bottom slewing).”

Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401].

Tilt up or tilt down operation means raising/lowering a load from the horizontal to vertical or vertical to horizontal. Tower crane is a type of lifting structure which utilizes a vertical mast or tower to support a working boom (jib) in an elevated position. Loads are suspended from the working boom. While the working boom may be of the fixed type (horizontal or angled) or have luffing capability, it can always rotate to swing loads, either by rotating on the top of the tower (top slewing) or by the rotation of the tower (bottom slewing).

§1926.1441(d)(2) Anti two-blocking “(2) Anti two-blocking. The employer must ensure that equipment covered by this section manufactured more than one year after November 8, 2010 have either an anti two-block device that meets the requirements of § 1926.1416(d)(3), or is designed so that, in the event of a two-block situation, no damage or load failure will occur (for example, by using a power unit that stalls in response to a two-block situation).” §1926.1436(g)(2)(iv) “(iv) Actuating the anti two-block and boom hoist limit devices (if provided).” §1926.1441 Equipment with a rated hoisting/lifting capacity of 2,000 pounds or less For equipment rated at 2,000 pounds or less, the employer must comply with listed subpart provisions, including ground conditions, assembly/disassembly, power lines, wire rope, signals, stop authority and fall protection [29cfr1926.1441(a)].

Assembly must also meet component, configuration and manufacturer-prohibition rules [29cfr1926.1441(b)(1)]. Choices affecting capacity or safe operation must follow manufacturer documents or meet approved-modification requirements. If manufacturer information is unavailable under the first route, a familiar registered professional engineer must give written approval [29cfr1926.1441(b)(2)(i)]. The equipment is inspected after assembly [29cfr1926.1441(b)(2)(ii)]. Applicable manufacturer prohibitions [29cfr1926.1441(b)(3)] and operating procedures, including attachment use, must be followed [29cfr1926.1441(c)(1)]. Missing procedures trigger development duties [29cfr1926.1441(c)(2)].

Keep in mind that the load chart must be at the control station, and procedures and manuals readily available. If electronic-only capacities become inaccessible through failure, the operator immediately ceases operations or follows safe shut-down procedures until capacities are available [29cfr1926.1441(c)(3)].

Original safety devices and aids are maintained, and equipment inspected, according to manufacturer procedures [29cfr1926.1441(d)(1)] [29cfr1926.1441(h)]. Equipment manufactured more than one year after November 8, 2010 needs compliant anti two-block protection or a protective design [29cfr1926.1441(d)(2)]. Operators need pre-operation training [29cfr1926.1441(e)], and signal persons need signal training [29cfr1926.1441(f)]. Hoisting personnel is prohibited [29cfr1926.1441(j)]. A qualified engineer must design the equipment [29cfr1926.1441(k)]. “(iii) When rated capacities are available at the control station only in electronic form and a failure occurs that makes the rated capacities inaccessible, the operator immediately ceases operations or follows safe shut-down procedures until the rated capacities (in electronic or other form) are available. (2) Anti two-blocking. The employer must ensure that equipment covered by this section manufactured more than one year after November 8, 2010 have either an anti two-block device that meets the requirements of § 1926.1416(d)(3), or is designed so that, in the event of a two-block situation, no damage or load failure will occur (for example, by using a power unit that stalls in response to a two-block situation).
(iv) Actuating the anti two-block and boom hoist limit devices (if provided).
§1926.1441 Equipment with a rated hoisting/lifting capacity of 2,000 pounds or less

For equipment rated at 2,000 pounds or less, the employer must comply with listed subpart provisions, including ground conditions, assembly/disassembly, power lines, wire rope, signals, stop authority and fall protection [29cfr1926.1441(a)].

Assembly must also meet component, configuration and manufacturer-prohibition rules [29cfr1926.1441(b)(1)]. Choices affecting capacity or safe operation must follow manufacturer documents or meet approved-modification requirements. If manufacturer information is unavailable under the first route, a familiar registered professional engineer must give written approval [29cfr1926.1441(b)(2)(i)]. The equipment is inspected after assembly [29cfr1926.1441(b)(2)(ii)]. Applicable manufacturer prohibitions [29cfr1926.1441(b)(3)] and operating procedures, including attachment use, must be followed [29cfr1926.1441(c)(1)]. Missing procedures trigger development duties [29cfr1926.1441(c)(2)].

Keep in mind that the load chart must be at the control station, and procedures and manuals readily available. If electronic-only capacities become inaccessible through failure, the operator immediately ceases operations or follows safe shut-down procedures until capacities are available [29cfr1926.1441(c)(3)].

Original safety devices and aids are maintained, and equipment inspected, according to manufacturer procedures [29cfr1926.1441(d)(1)] [29cfr1926.1441(h)]. Equipment manufactured more than one year after November 8, 2010 needs compliant anti two-block protection or a protective design [29cfr1926.1441(d)(2)]. Operators need pre-operation training [29cfr1926.1441(e)], and signal persons need signal training [29cfr1926.1441(f)]. Hoisting personnel is prohibited [29cfr1926.1441(j)]. A qualified engineer must design the equipment [29cfr1926.1441(k)].

(iii) When rated capacities are available at the control station only in electronic form and a failure occurs that makes the rated capacities inaccessible, the operator immediately ceases operations or follows safe shut-down procedures until the rated capacities (in electronic or other form) are available. §1910.179 Overhead and gantry cranes Only designated personnel operate [29cfr1910.179(b)(8)]. Stay within rated load except for tests [29cfr1910.179(n)(1)]; test loads are limited to 125 percent unless the manufacturer recommends otherwise [29cfr1910.179(k)(2)]. Each shift, try every upper hoist limit under no load, inching or slowly; immediately notify the appointed person of faults. Never use it as an operating control [29cfr1910.179(n)(4)].

Check rope, lines and hook position before hoisting; secure and balance loads; avoid sudden speed changes and obstructions. Side pulls need specific authorization. No movement with employees on load or hook. Avoid carrying loads over people, test brakes near rated load, keep two full drum wraps, stay at controls, and sound warnings when required. Multi-crane lifts need one qualified responsible person in charge [29cfr1910.179(n)(3)].

Frequent inspections run daily to monthly, periodic 1 to 12 months [29cfr1910.179(j)(1)(ii)]. Voltage: control 600, pendant 150 AC/300 DC, cab-crane receptacle 300 [29cfr1910.179(g)]. §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Boom (tower cranes): On tower cranes, if the “boom” (i.e., principal horizontal structure) is fixed, it is referred to as a jib; if it is moveable up and down, it is referred to as a boom. Boom angle indicator means a device which measures the angle of the boom relative to horizontal. Boom hoist limiting device includes boom hoist disengaging device, boom hoist shut-off, boom hoist disconnect, boom hoist hydraulic relief, boom hoist kick-outs, automatic boom stop device, or derricking limiter.”

§1926.1441(c)(2)(iii) “(iii) Ensure that procedures related to the capacity of the equipment are developed and signed by a registered professional engineer familiar with the equipment.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “It compares this lifting condition to the equipment's rated capacity, and when the rated capacity is reached, it shuts off power to those equipment functions which can increase the severity of loading on the equipment, e.g., hoisting, telescoping out, or luffing out. Typically, those functions which decrease the severity of loading on the equipment remain operational, e.g., lowering, telescoping in, or luffing in. Locomotive crane means a crane mounted on a base or car equipped for travel on a railroad track.”

§1926.1427 Operator training, certification, and evaluation Covered equipment requires training, certification or licensing, and evaluation; otherwise, you operate only as a supervised trainee [29cfr1926.1427(a)(1)]. Derricks, sidebooms and equipment rated 2,000 pounds or less are excepted, but their training rules remain [29cfr1926.1427(a)(2)]. Military qualifications are employer-specific and last as the issuer stipulates [29cfr1926.1427(a)(3)].

Trainees need formal and practical instruction, assigned tasks within their ability, and continuous on-site monitoring by a qualified employer employee or agent doing nothing distracting [29cfr1926.1427(b)]. Non-tower cranes require line of sight plus verbal or hand signals; tower cranes require direct communication. Breaks are limited to 15 minutes, one per hour, after a task-and-limits briefing, with tasks within ability [29cfr1926.1427(b)(4)]. Uncertified trainees cannot work where equipment, line or load at maximum radius could reach within 20 feet of power lines up to 350 kV, or 50 feet above that voltage. They also cannot hoist personnel, make multiple-equipment lifts, or work over shafts or cofferdams or in tank farms. Multiple-lift rigging is barred unless the trainer finds their skills sufficient [29cfr1926.1427(b)(3)].

Qualifying state or local licensing governs within its jurisdiction (maximum validity 5 years); otherwise certification is required, with no employee cost [29cfr1926.1427(c)]. Accredited certification is type-based or type-and-capacity-based, portable among employers required to use that option, and valid 5 years; accreditation review occurs at least every 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(d)]. Audited-employer certification lasts 5 years and is not portable [29cfr1926.1427(e)(6)]. Audits occur within 3 months of program start, then at least every 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(e)(3)]. Significant deficiencies halt qualification until confirmed correction, require re-audit within 180 days afterward and an auditor's OSHA report within 15 days of determination; auditors keep audit records 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(e)(5)].

Evaluation covers safe operation, equipment-specific features and assigned hoisting [29cfr1926.1427(f)(1)]. Other equipment is allowed if the employer can demonstrate no substantially different abilities are needed [29cfr1926.1427(f)(5)]. Performance or knowledge evaluation indicating a need triggers retraining and subject re-evaluation [29cfr1926.1427(b)(5)] [29cfr1926.1427(f)(7)]. Pre-December 10, 2018 employees may be covered by prior assessments [29cfr1926.1427(f)(2)]. The section's effective date is December 10, 2018; evaluation and documentation, February 7, 2019 [29cfr1926.1427(k)]. “(2) Exceptions. Operators of derricks (see § 1926.1436), sideboom cranes (see § 1926.1440), or equipment with a maximum manufacturer-rated hoisting/lifting capacity of 2,000 pounds or less (see § 1926.1441) are not required to comply with § 1926.1427. Note: The training requirements in those other sections continue to apply (for the training requirement for operators of sideboom cranes, follow section 1926.1430(c)). (3) Qualification by the U.S.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Dismantling includes partial dismantling (such as dismantling to shorten a boom or substitute a different component). Drum rotation indicator means a device on a crane or hoist which indicates in which direction and at what relative speed a particular hoist drum is turning. Electrical contact occurs when a person, object, or equipment makes contact or comes in close proximity with an energized conductor or equipment that allows the passage of current. Employer-made equipment means floating cranes/derricks designed and built by an employer for the employer's own use.”

These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Drum rotation indicator means a device on a crane or hoist which indicates in which direction and at what relative speed a particular hoist drum is turning. Table T to §1926.1411 Table T—Minimum Clearance Distances While Traveling With No Load “Table T—Minimum Clearance Distances While Traveling With No Load Voltage (nominal, kV, alternating current) | While traveling—minimum clearance distance (feet) up to 0.75 | 4 over .75 to 50 | 6 over 50 to 345 | 10 over 345 to 750 | 16 Over 750 to 1,000 | 20 Over 1,000 | (as established by the utility owner/operator or registered professional engineer who is a qualified person with respect to electrical power transmission and distribution).” Table A to §1926.1408 Table A—Minimum Clearance Distances “Table A—Minimum Clearance Distances Voltage (nominal, kV, alternating current) | Minimum clearance distance (feet) up to 50 | 10 over 50 to 200 | 15 over 200 to 350 | 20 over 350 to 500 | 25 over 500 to 750 | 35 over 750 to 1,000 | 45 over 1,000 | (as established by the utility owner/operator or registered professional engineer who is a qualified person with respect to electrical power transmission and distribution). Note: The value that follows “to” is up to and includes that value. For example, over 50 to 200 means up to and including 200kV.” §1926.1411 Power line safety—while traveling under or near power lines with no load These procedures and criteria cover equipment traveling with no load under or near a power line on a construction site. Loaded travel falls under § 1926.1408, § 1926.1409 or § 1926.1410, whichever is appropriate, and § 1926.1417(u) [29cfr1926.1411(a)].

The employer must ensure the boom/mast and its support system are lowered sufficiently [29cfr1926.1411(b)(1)], Table T clearances are maintained [29cfr1926.1411(b)(2)], and speed and terrain effects, including boom/mast movement, are considered so they do not cause a breach of minimum clearance [29cfr1926.1411(b)(3)].

Table T minimums, by nominal AC voltage in kV, are: up to 0.75, 4 feet; over .75 to 50, 6 feet; over 50 to 345, 10 feet; over 345 to 750, 16 feet; over 750 to 1,000, 20 feet. Over 1,000, the distance is established by the utility owner/operator or a registered professional engineer qualified in electrical power transmission and distribution [29cfr1926.1411-table-T].

The intervals in turn are dependent upon the nature of the critical components of the crane and the degree of their exposure to wear, deterioration, or malfunction. The two general classifications are herein designated as “frequent” and “periodic”, with respective intervals between inspections as defined below: (i) Frequent inspection: Daily to monthly intervals. (ii) Periodic inspection: 1- to 12-month intervals, or as specifically recommended by the manufacturer.

(i) A crane which has been idle for a period of one month or more, but less than 6 months, shall be given an inspection conforming with requirements of paragraph (d)(3) of this section and paragraph (g)(2)(ii) of this section before placing in service.
(xvii) Warning labels and decals originally supplied with the equipment by the manufacturer or otherwise required under this standard: Missing or unreadable.

A decision point concerns engineering: where the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure that it is provided [29cfr1926.1432(a)(3)].

Under the wording of that paragraph, a competent person who does not also meet the qualified person criteria needs that assistance to fit either arrangement.
